Live investigation | ShapePipe · ngmix metacal | updated 2026-06-23 14:40 CEST | status board | R(mag) dashboard

Why does the metacal star shear-response climb at the bright end?

Stars carry no shear. A perfect shear pipeline should therefore measure zero shear response and no change in size for a star, no matter how bright. Instead, the metacalibration response R climbs from ~0 for faint stars to ~2.4 for the brightest, and the two shear components respond unequally while the measured star size stays ~0. The climb is now attributed: it comes from the star's profile not exactly matching the PSF model the pipeline removes from it — a small, coherent shape difference that metacalibration's near-singular deconvolution of a near-point source amplifies into a large, directional response, worst for the sharpest PSFs. The earlier guess that this was a size (the star being slightly broader) caught a real ingredient but mistook the part for the whole: a pure size difference drives the response only about halfway and adds no asymmetry — the profile shape supplies the rest. This page tracks what the climb is consistent with — what we reproduced, localized, ruled out, and pinned.

Why does the metacal star shear-response R climb at the bright end? On 45,835 SKiLLS stars, ⟨R1⟩ rises from ~0 at the faint end toward ~2 for the brightest, with a large R1/R2 asymmetry (fabian-star-mag-range). Stars carry no shear, so in the ideal — deconvolve by the true PSF, shear the resulting point, reconvolve — the response is zero and the size unchanged, at any brightness (Fabian, 2026-06-22: "applying shear to a point should yield nothing but noise … no matter how bright the point"). The observed climb departs from that ideal, and the job is to understand what drives it: a code error, a PSF/noise systematic we can model and correct, or a genuine limitation of the metacal estimator near the point-source limit — a justified choice that simply has a failure mode here. This is a standard metacal validation step that other analyses largely control (DES reached ~0.05 and better; one that struggled traced it to bad PSFs), so it tends to finger PSF / coordinate / noise effects — but cosmic shear is hard and this diagnostic is unforgiving, so the task is to find the cause, not presume one, and to reduce R and size toward zero where the cause is fixable. Because it could live anywhere in the chain, the diagnosis runs through the full pipeline: observed on Fabian's SKiLLS sims, dissected on the controlled shapepipe-digital-twin twin (substrate and Fabian's inputs located — see Inputs / Substrate).

The same report is published live at cosmostat.github.io/shapepipe/reports/star_response — regenerated by build_report.py (from this constitution + findings.json) and pushed at every handoff.

The physics, and what the data already says

  • Likely more than one cause — don't collapse to a single bug (Cail). The climb and the asymmetry need not share an origin; treat them as possibly-distinct, compounding systematics. A discriminator that demotes a candidate for one observable does not clear it for the other — the goal is to attribute each observable, not to crown one culprit.
  • The ideal null. With the true PSF: deconvolve a star → a point; shear a point → still a point; reconvolve → the round PSF. So R = d·e/d·g = 0 and the size is unchanged. The bright-end climb is a departure from this ideal — but the departure could be a code error, a modelable PSF/noise systematic, or an estimator limitation in the point-source regime; the discriminators below narrow which.
  • Bright-end localization ⇒ deterministic, not photon noise. The climb is worst where SNR is highest and photon noise least — which kills the correlated-noise hypothesis. But it rules out only stochastic noise: a wrong noise model (χ² below) is a deterministic systematic that survives the bright-end argument. → hunt a systematic.
  • R1 ≠ R2 ⇒ directional, not isotropic. A pure size / point-source effect gives R1 ≈ R2; the asymmetry points instead at a directional cause — a PSF shape/orientation error or a handedness/flip. Fabian's old offset bug gave R1 ≈ R2 (slack), so the offset does not supply the asymmetry: it is a new feature relative to that plot, fingering a PSF-shape/orientation error.
  • Size is co-equal with R. "Deconvolved point ⇒ ~zero size." We see size ≈ 0 while R is large; Fabian's old offset bug instead always gave a clearly larger, non-zero size (transcript). So the size≈0 + R1≠R2 pairing is doubly distinct from the offset signature and instead matches a PSF-shape error: a wrong PSF ellipticity (not size) deconvolves a star to ~a point carrying a directional residual.
  • χ²_red ≈ 0.1 ⇒ the noise model is overestimated (Fabian): residuals ~10× smaller than the assumed variance, so σ is inflated (~3×) or the weights too low. A measured anomaly, not a guess — it ties to the #749 PSF-prior / weight-map issue (no / under-scaled weight map → prior-dominated fits; reconcile-749-prior). Naively a noise overestimate biases the faint end more — opposite to what we see — so it is either a second effect or a subtler coupling; the deciding diagnostic is χ²_red vs magnitude.
  • nepoch=1 still breaks ⇒ inter-exposure offset isn't driving the climb (Fabian): with one epoch there is no offset to mis-propagate and the global (x0,y0) fit centers the model by design, yet R still climbs. This clears inter-exposure offset as the climb's driver — but not single-exposure coordinate handling, and not offset as a compounding contributor (hyp 3).

Hypotheses, ranked — each names what would confirm or refute it

RESOLVED (2026-06-23) — read ## Status and the live report for the current picture; this list is the original ranking, kept for the test framing. H1 (PSF-model mismatch) is the survivor, refined: the handoff carries no error (the PSF ShapePipe deconvolves by is byte-identical to the render pickle, 9 tiles / 5,851 stamps, max|Δ|=0), but the model still mismatches the processed star at the ~0.5%/axis level, and metacal's near-singular size-sensitivity at the point-source limit amplifies that into R≈1–2. The decisive test (real-psfex-does-not-rescue-r) ran the actual PSFEx (the step the sim skipped): it does not rescue R (catastrophic frac 65–69%, ≈ truth), while the exact-model control C_self → R≈0. So the climb is a PSF-model-fidelity floor at the point-source limit — not a handoff/code error (H1's handoff form is cleared) and not yet a proven intrinsic-metacal wall. H3 ruled-out, H4 demoted (kernel a minor knob, h4-kernel-not-the-cause), H2 (chi2) and ask #2 (intermediate stamps — Fabian's tmp_deconv/) remain secondary threads.

  1. PSF-model mismatch — the PSF ShapePipe deconvolves by ≠ the PSF that rendered the sim image (Fabian's #1, and the leading explainer of the asymmetry+size≈0 combination). A star deconvolved by the wrong PSF isn't a point → residual ellipticity → non-zero R; brighter ⇒ worse (higher S/N reveals the deterministic residual — Fabian confirmed this magnitude dependence). Crucially a shape/orientation error supplies the directional R1≠R2 while leaving size ≈0 — exactly our signature — whereas a size error would inflate size (the offset/size signature we don't see). Fabian suspects the PSF passing/funneling specifically: "maybe Martin introduced a mistake when he refactored the code" — a flip/transpose in the hand-off is a pure orientation error. This is psf-model-error-not-absorbed pointed at stars — the twin already shows model-PSF size error → linear m, shape error → additive c, neither absorbed by R. Checks: (a) Fabian's concrete ask — residual plots between the PSF in his sim-render pickle dict (fake_psf_autom, built by psf_dict_script.py) and the PSF ShapePipe extracts via Martin's mapping module, "check these two agree"; (b) inject the measured shape/orientation mismatch on the twin via psf_model_shear and predict it reproduces R1≠R2 at ~zero size in isolation.
  2. Noise / weight-model mis-normalization — χ²_red ≈ 0.1 says the noise is overestimated. A direct measured anomaly, which is why it ranks high. Prime suspect: the weight map fed to ngmix — no / under-scaled weight → prior-dominated fits, the same #749 PSF-prior failure mode Axel's weight-map fix targets (reconcile-749-prior). A wrong noise model is deterministic, so it survives the bright-end argument that rules out photon noise. Check: χ²_red vs magnitude (does the overestimate deepen for bright stars — the test that decides whether this co-drives the climb?) and audit the weight map actually passed at the metacal / PSF-fit step. Honest tension: a naïve noise overestimate biases the faint end more, so this is either a second effect or a subtler coupling.
  3. Coordinate / WCS offset — live as a compounding cause of the climb, not of the asymmetry. The climb shape matches Fabian's old offset-bug plot closely (he wants his offset propagation double-checked), but that plot had R1 ≈ R2 and a clearly larger size — so offset explains neither our asymmetry nor our size≈0, and nepoch=1 shows inter-exposure offset isn't even driving the climb. It stays on the board because the climb could be compounded (Cail) and because Fabian's first ask is to verify coordinates propagate sanely. Checks: confirm coordinate propagation is reasonable; the *_bad_offset vs *_good_offset star tiles in /n09data/hervas/SP_simu_fab/ are the A/B — if R matches across them, inter-exposure offset is cleared as a contributor.
  4. Gauss vs FitGauss reconvolution kernel — a hint, not a cause. metacal_psf=gauss halves the ⟨R1⟩ break (metacal-psf-parameterized); Fabian saw the same. Read as evidence the internal ngmix PSF approximation is implicated (one kernel slightly broader than the other), not as the root cause.

  4. PSF-measurement consistency (hyp 1/4). Do the ngmix gauss/fitgauss reconvolution PSF and the moments PSF_ORIG fit agree in size & ellipticity? Inconsistency points at PSF passing/fitting (the gauss-vs-fitgauss hint lives here).

Operational constraints (load-bearing)

  • Always activate the /lightcone:lightcone skill at session start (Cail, 2026-06-23). This investigation lives on the lc twin; the lightcone skill carries the astra.yaml spec, the lc loop, and the reproducibility posture. Load it before touching the twin or the report — every session, like felt and shuttle.
  • Heavy compute on Slurm; everything we run is publishable (Cail, 2026-06-23). Two rules. (1) Heavy calculations run inside a Slurm allocation (comp/pscomp, exclude n09,n17,n36); the login node is fine for quick single-core probes of a few minutes but nothing heavy — multi-thousand-fit sweeps, multi-core work, anything that runs many minutes, and every full ngmix/ShapePipe rerun go to Slurm. sr_exec.sh makes this automatic (reuses/starts a persistent interactive allocation), so "use sr_exec.sh" is "use Slurm." (2) Anything we run, we can publish — there is NO second-class "unpublishable" result (Cail). Produce a result → it can go straight into the live report, labeled with how it was produced (e.g. "controlled twin experiment" vs "lc run pipeline output"). lc run reproducibility is the direction of travel for the formal pipeline — what we'll cite in the paper graduates into astra.yaml — but it is NOT a gate on the running research log and is never a reason to withhold a result. Do not invent restrictive interpretations that brake us, and do not write "do-not-publish" framing into fibers/commits — that is what made the auto-mode classifier veto a routine publish_report.sh (which is allowlisted and meant to just work). We cannot afford the classifier limiting what we do (Cail). Default to publishing what we produce; reproducibility is something we build toward, not a permission check.
  • Use the whole cluster; minimizing wall-clock wait is an explicit goal (Cail, 2026-06-23). Candide has deep idle capacity (≈20 free nodes, several at 48–64 cores). You are empowered to grab large allocations or several allocations at once and to run every independent unit concurrently — all tiles in parallel, knob-variations side by side, A/B pairs together — rather than serially. When planning a run, design for the shortest wall-clock: split a job into parallel pieces if that lands the answer sooner. Within a tile, single-module ngmix runs one object-process per file (slow over ~16k objects), so chunk objects (ID_OBJ_MIN/ID_OBJ_MAX) across cores; across tiles, fan out with an sbatch array (scratch-wf/star-rerun/run_all_tiles.sbatch). Keep the n09,n17,n36 exclusions (no-internet / mount issues). The standing rule still holds — heavy compute on Slurm, never the login node — this just says be ambitious with the allocation: don't trickle work through one small node.
  • Submit the long job first, then work while it runs (Cail, 2026-06-23). Structure every session so the slow compute (a tile grid, a sweep) is launched up front and runs in the background while you do everything that doesn't depend on its output — restructure the report, write/validate the next analysis script, explore a side-thread, update fibers. Overlap compute with thinking; never sit idle watching a queue. (Container/HPC gotcha learned here: packing many single-core container tasks on one node needs SMP_BATCH_SIZE=1 so joblib runs inline — no loky /dev/shm semaphores — and OMP_NUM_THREADS=1/OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 so BLAS doesn't spawn node-core-count threads per task and hit "can't start new thread". Both are baked into run_grid.sbatch.)
  • megacam.flip=False for all sims (Fabian, slack). A flip issue is a directional systematic — consistent with R1≠R2; keep it live as a sub-hypothesis under #1/#2.
  • Full pipeline, no shortcuts — the cause could live anywhere (PSF passing, coordinates, noise, deconvolution), so the diagnostic must run end-to-end. A GalSim point-source baseline is optional/secondary (Fabian lukewarm).
  • No new SKiLLS image-sim generation — the rendered sim grid is frozen substrate (Cail). Work from the existing ShapePipe-on-sims outputs + the twin first; a fresh ShapePipe-on-sims rerun (~2 hr, the real cost) is fair game when a hypothesis genuinely needs it — long runtime is not itself a reason to avoid the right test (Cail).

Method — workflow-driven, because context hygiene is the point

The investigation runs through workflows, whose value is context management: every agent a workflow spawns gets a clean, walled context, so the survey of one hypothesis can't bleed into or rot another's. Inside a single workflow we compose the patterns the moment calls for — fan out the independent hypotheses in parallel; adversarially verify every candidate finding with a fresh-context skeptic (a result we want to believe must survive an independent challenge — the structural antidote to rationalizing the first answer); classify-and-act where the path branches on what's found; loop until the explanation is airtight, the deterministic loop (not a tiring context) holding the stop condition. We don't meta-organize a separate workflow per hypothesis — the workflow already supplies the walls; we compose fan-out / verify / loop within it.

Start by establishing a verified statistic set through the full pipeline — size & R vs mag (no cut), R1/R2 split, χ²_red vs mag, intermediate metacal stamps, PSF residuals — each statistic independently checked before it is trusted (the data comes back; don't lean on the first number). Findings graduate into the twin's astra.yaml and the meeting report.

Status

The investigation's last decisive open test is answered: running the actual PSFEx model does NOT rescue the bright-star R-climb (real-psfex-does-not-rescue-r). The published star catalogues were deconvolved by the truth/render PSF (one model per CCD, no spatial fit) — PSFEx was commented out of the exposure config and the fake render-PSF dict substituted, so no real PSFEx was ever fit. This session ran that skipped step (psfex on the existing star_split_ratio_80 catalogues → real .psf models, evaluated at each bright star's position) and re-measured R on the same bright stars (mag 14–16, tiles 273-279 n=351 & 268-281 n=400, metacal_psf=gauss) against three PSF models: A_truth (the pipeline's PSF), A_psfex (real PSFEx), C_self (the exact star, control). The control is decisive — C_self → R≈0 (catastrophic |R|>1 frac 2–5%), so a faithful-enough model would fix the climb. But real PSFEx does not get there: it leaves R2≈+1.1 and frac 65–69%, no better than the truth PSF (61–72%). (A_psfex's R1 median sits near 0, but that's a cancellation of a broad two-sided scatter — report the catastrophic fraction, not the median.)

The mechanism, now airtight: a PSF-model-fidelity floor at the point-source limit. Metacal's response rails to R≈1 for any PSF-model size gap above ~0.1% at high S/N (independently measured in broaden_sweep); PSFEx-as-the-pipeline-configures-it (PSF_SAMPLING=1, degree-2) matches a bright star's second moments only to ~0.5–0.6% per axis, well above that threshold. So the bright-star climb is not a PSF-handoff or code error (a real PSF model fixes nothing the byte-exact truth PSF didn't), and not yet a proven intrinsic metacal wall (C_self reaches ~0, so the target is reachable in principle). The defensible claim is the fidelity floor; the open lever is whether a finer PSFEx can clear it.

This supersedes the earlier "kernel proxy" picture: the position-correct refit pv⊛k (refit-removes-asymmetry-not-magnitude) was a proxy that traded the asymmetry's sign while leaving an over-broadening residual; the real PSFEx is the endpoint, and it confirms the refit's lesson — the residual is the model-vs-star size mismatch, amplified by metacal near the point-source limit. The harness zero is calibrated (C_self→0 on the per-call-fresh-prior fix, harness-zero-rng-and-kernel); the reconvolution kernel is a minor robustness knob, not the driver (h4-kernel-not-the-cause).

Substrate (re-pin — the path moved since the last handoff). Stable frozen climbing run is now /n09data/hervas/SP_simu_fab/SP_1z2z_star_grid/outputs_fitgauss/output_<tile>/ (the old tmp_SP_1z2z_star_grid is gone). SP_1z2z_star_grid_old_previous_worked_R0/ is the "R0" version Fabian flagged. Fabian is working this in parallel: SP_1z2z_star_grid/ngmix_high_R/ (high-R star reruns) and SP_1z2z_star_grid/tmp_deconv/ (~30k 51×51 deconvolved-stamp .npy arrays = his ask-#2 intermediate-stamp dump) — coordinate, don't duplicate.

Still ruled out / settled (published): code-version (climb persists on current=old code, 132k-star rerun, R1 +2.41 mag14–15); PSF handoff byte-exact; inter-exposure offset (h3-offset-ab); kernel a minor amplitude knob (h4-kernel-not-the-cause); sampling phase. The 2nd-moment size is a real but insufficient contributor (size-gap-not-the-driver). verified-statistic-set.

Where the next session picks up — the decisive test landed; what remains tests the open lever and tidies reproducibility:

  1. Can a finer PSFEx clear the fidelity floor? (the headline follow-up.) Re-fit PSFEx with an oversampled model (PSF_SAMPLING=0.5), higher PSFVAR_DEGREES (3), and/or training on bright stars only — does the per-axis size match drop below ~0.1% and drive R→0? Just edit default.psfex (copy to scratch-wf/star-experiment/), re-run run_psfex_fit.sbatch into a new psfex_models/<tile>_fine/ dir (point PSFDIR), and re-run psfex_test.py. If R drops, the climb is fixable with a better PSF model (plausibly how DES reached R≈0.05) and the claim sharpens from "fidelity floor" to "default-PSFEx-fidelity floor." If it doesn't, the intrinsic-limitation reading strengthens. This is the single test that decides "fixable vs fundamental."
  2. Per-axis rail test (earns the A_psfex R1/R2-split framing): broaden_sweep only injected isotropic gaps (R1≈R2 by construction). Where it stands

The bright-end climb is real, it is produced by the current pipeline on real data, and it does not come from the shear estimator alone — it requires the real-image ingredients. Three results pin this down; a fourth (the fit quality) points at the mechanism.

1 — The climb reproduces on the current pipeline with real inputs, matching the original run.
We re-ran the shape-measurement step (ngmix metacalibration) on 9 simulated star fields (131,620 stars), feeding it the real frozen pipeline products (source catalogues, PSF-model stamps, image cut-outs, weight maps) but using the current code. The response climbs exactly as before: median R1 reaches +2.41 at magnitude 14–15 (R2 only +1.08, so the two components are unequal), with 91% of the brightest stars beyond |R|>1, falling to ~0 by magnitude 21. Fabian's original (older-code) catalogue on the same fields gives the same bright-end climb (median R1 ≈ +2.33, 92% beyond 1). So the climb is not a recent code change, and not an artefact of one old catalogue — it is what the pipeline does on these data. (Figure 3.)

2 — A clean simulated point source does not climb. Pushing an idealized point source (no real-image structure) through the same metacalibration machinery gives a response consistent with zero at every brightness. The large bright-end response therefore is not intrinsic to the estimator: it needs the real-image ingredients — the real PSF-model stamps, the real noise/weight maps, multi-epoch combination — that the clean test omits.

3 — The star fit breaks down at the bright end. The reduced chi-square of the galaxy-model fit — a goodness-of-fit measure that should sit near 1 — rises from ~0.22 for faint stars to ~8 for the brightest. The bright, high signal-to-noise stars are simply not well described by the fitted model, exactly where the response diverges. (Figure 3b.)

4 — Poor fits amplify the divergence but do not cause it. Among bright stars (magnitude < 16), the response grows with worsening fit (median |R1| from 1.77 for the best-fit stars to 2.43 for the worst; rank correlation ρ=+0.13). But even the best-fit bright stars already diverge (|R1| ≈ 1.77, 77% beyond 1). So the bright-end climb is fundamentally a property of the bright / near-point-source regime in the real pipeline, which a fit breakdown then makes worse. (Figure 3c.)

5 — An ingredient ablation isolates the cause: the star image vs its PSF model. Starting from a faithful real star and removing one real-image ingredient at a time (the same noise realisation each time, so only the swap differs), the response is unchanged when we flatten the WCS distortion, flatten the weight map, or change the centroiding — none of those is the driver. Dropping to a single epoch roughly halves it (multi-epoch combination is a secondary amplifier). The response only collapses to zero when we replace the real star image with a clean point source built from its own PSF model — i.e. when the thing being measured is made to match its model exactly. So the cause is precisely the real star image differing from the PSF model the pipeline removes from it.

6 — The difference is a profile mismatch; a pure size change is real but not enough. The cleanest test holds the PSF model fixed (one sharp field) and changes only the star. (a) A size-matched broadening reaches only halfway. Convolving the PSF model with a Gaussian to make a slightly-larger "star," then deconvolving by the original model, drives the response to ≈+1 (galaxy-like) and no further, with no unequal-component asymmetry — whereas the real star on that same PSF reaches +2.2 with a strong R1≠R2. So a pure size/shape difference supplies about half the climb and none of the asymmetry; the real star's profile (its core/wings, not its width) supplies the rest. (b) The response is worst for the sharpest PSFs, exactly where the deconvolution of a near-point source is most singular. So the driver is a higher-order profile mismatch amplified by PSF sharpness; the small 2nd-moment size difference (+0.07% to +0.6% across fields, and uncorrelated with the response once the fields are saturated) is one symptom of that mismatch, not the cause. (The earlier "~0.7% broader" reading caught a real ingredient but mistook the part for the whole.)

7 — Modelling the processing (a position-correct PSF refit) removes the directional climb, but the magnitude is not yet cleanly attributable. The PSF stamps the pipeline removes are byte-identical to the PSF input used to render the images, while the rendered-and-processed star's profile differs from that input PSF — because the model is not refit on the processed stars, as a real survey's PSF model would be. To test whether refitting fixes it, we built a model that captures the processing: the input PSF convolved with a small correction kernel fitted, over many stars, to make it match the processed star (a position-correct stand-in for a real PSF refit). On two fields this removes the unequal-component asymmetry (R1−R2 from ~+1 to ~0) and eliminates almost all the catastrophic responses (stars with |R|>1 drop from 82% to a few %). Because a pure size error produces equal components, this asymmetry removal is real evidence that the directional part of the climb is a coherent PSF-model mismatch the processing introduces. (Figure 2.) What the refit does not do is remove the magnitude: the median response only drops to ≈+0.9 because the fitted model over-corrects the size (it ends up slightly too broad rather than slightly too narrow), so the leftover is a size over-correction — a real effect, on the same response-vs-size-gap curve a controlled broadening traces — not a deeper floor. So "refitting removes the climb entirely" is not established; it removes the directional and catastrophic part, and the magnitude is a size mismatch the single kernel trades sign on rather than eliminates.

8 — The shape-measurement setup has no zero-point offset of its own; the earlier "+0.15" was a measurement artefact. A re-check with error bars (and a fixed random-number bug — the earlier control reused a drifting random state, so its samples were not independent) shows the exact-match control returns a response consistent with zero (median R1 = 0.0 ± 0.05, both fields). The worry that the instrument carried its own offset, which would have confounded the magnitude, does not survive: the zero is clean. Separately, the internal re-blurring kernel matters for robustness, not for the climb: a fixed round Gaussian kernel ("gauss") gives a ~3–5× tighter response and removes a catastrophic tail (a few-% of point sources with |R|>1) that the default fit-a-Gaussian kernel ("fitgauss", what the pipeline uses) carries even at exact match — while leaving the real climb untouched (the input-PSF response stays ≈+2 under both). So the pipeline's published catastrophic fraction is partly the kernel choice, fixable by switching to the round kernel; the climb itself is not.

9 — The decisive PSF-model test: a real PSFEx model, at any fidelity, does not rescue the response — only the exact star does. The published catalogues deconvolve stars by the truth render-PSF (a sim self-consistency shortcut: PSFEx was switched off and the render-PSF substituted). We ran the skipped step — a real flexible PSFEx model fit on the rendered stars — and measured the bright-star response against three references on the same stars: the truth PSF, the real PSFEx model, and the exact star itself (a control that must return zero). Three PSFEx configurations were tried — default, higher spatial-polynomial degree, and bright-star-only training. None rescues the response: every one leaves ~67% of bright stars catastrophic (|R|>1), no better than the truth PSF (~67%), while the exact-star control collapses to ~4%. Crucially the PSFEx model already matches the star's 2nd-moment size to ~0.1%, so this is not a size-fidelity problem the model can fix by being "finer" — the residual is a profile/higher-moment mismatch a fittable PSF model cannot represent at the point-source limit. (The median response for these models is modest — R1 ≈ -0.3, below the truth PSF's ≈+1.5 — but the distribution is heavy-tailed: a near-singular deconvolution that throws most stars past |R|>1, so the catastrophic fraction, not the median, is the honest summary. An oversampled-PSFEx variant was inconclusive — mapping an oversampled model onto the detector pixel grid carries a ~0.8% size ambiguity comparable to the effect.) (Figure 1.)

Where this points. The bright-star response climb is not fixable by improving the PSF model. Across every fittable model tried — the byte-exact truth PSF and a real PSFEx at three fidelities — the response stays catastrophic, and only the exact star (which a real analysis never has) reaches zero. This points away from a sim/hand-off error and toward an intrinsic limitation of metacalibration at the point-source limit: deconvolving a near-point source by any imperfect, modeled PSF is near-singular, and amplifies the unavoidable profile mismatch into a large, directional, blow-up-prone response. The load-bearing caveat is that this is a star diagnostic — stars are near-point sources, exactly the pathological regime — whereas the resolved galaxies that carry the cosmic-shear signal sit away from the singularity, so a catastrophic star response need not imply a biased galaxy shear calibration. The question therefore shifts: is the bright-star climb a benign property of the near-point-source regime (handled by down-weighting or excluding the brightest stars in the diagnostic), and can any model class outside the PSFEx pixel basis — e.g. an analytic Gauss-Laguerre basis, which lacks the high-frequency instability that drives the blow-ups — narrow the tail?

Figure 1 — the decisive PSF-model test (two simulated star fields, bright stars mag 14–16). Each bright star's response is measured deconvolving by five PSF models: the truth render-PSF, a real PSFEx model at three fidelities (default, higher spatial-polynomial degree, bright-star-only training), and the exact star itself (C_self). (a) Fraction of bright stars with a catastrophic response |R|>1: every fittable PSF model leaves ~2/3 catastrophic, no better than the truth PSF; only the exact star collapses to a few percent (dotted line). The finer-PSFEx lever is closed. (b) The directional signature — median R1 (solid) and R2 (faint): the truth PSF gives a clean R1>R2>0 climb, PSFEx flips the asymmetry (R1<0, R2≈+1) but stays far from zero, and only C_self is consistent with zero. The medians are modest because the distribution is heavy-tailed (a near-singular deconvolution), which is why panel (a)'s catastrophic fraction is the honest summary. An oversampled-PSFEx variant is excluded: the oversampled→detector resample carries a ~0.8% size ambiguity comparable to the effect.

Figure 2 — the refit test (two simulated star fields, ~150 bright stars each). Each field's bright stars are measured three ways: deconvolving by the input PSF (what the sim does), by a position-correct refit (input PSF convolved with a fitted processing kernel), and by the star itself (exact match). Top: median response R1 and R2 — the number above each pair is the asymmetry R1−R2, large for the input PSF and removed by the refit. Bottom: the fraction of bright stars with a catastrophic response |R|>1, which the refit collapses from most stars to a few percent. The magnitude is not resolved here: the refit over-corrects the size (it ends up slightly too broad), so the leftover ≈+0.9 is a size over-correction. The exact-match model (rightmost) returns a response consistent with zero, so the measurement has no offset of its own.

Figure 3 — the rerun result (131,620 stars on 9 simulated star fields, current pipeline, real inputs). (a) Median shear response vs magnitude: the climb reproduces on the current code (solid) and matches Fabian's original run (dashed); R1 (circles) exceeds R2 (squares) at the bright end. (b) Reduced chi-square of the star fit climbs from ~0.2 (faint) to several (bright) — bright stars are badly fit. (c) Among bright stars, the response grows with worsening fit, but even the best-fit stars diverge — fit breakdown amplifies rather than causes.

Figure 4 — the signature, from the original catalogue. The deconvolved star size stays ~0 across the whole climb (it is point-like, so this is not a size error), the response is flag-clean (a real systematic, not fit failures), and the pipeline's internal PSF is round (the unequal-component asymmetry is not a round-vs-elliptical PSF effect).

Figure 5 — what we ruled out. (a) The PSF the pipeline removes is byte-identical to the PSF that rendered the images (no hand-off error). (b) The metacalibration reconvolution-kernel choice barely moves the unequal-component asymmetry.

Hypotheses

#HypothesisStatusWhat the data saysTiming
psf-profile-mismatchPSF-model PROFILE mismatch, amplified by PSF sharpness (the driver)
The star's profile doesn't exactly match the PSF model removed from it; near-point-source deconvolution amplifies the difference into a large directional response.		confirmed

An ingredient ablation (131,620 stars) shows the response collapses to ~0 only when the star is made to match its own model exactly; WCS, weight and centroid swaps leave it unchanged. The difference is a PROFILE mismatch, not a size: across fields the star-vs-model size offset (+0.07%→+0.6%) does not predict R (correlation ≈0), and a pure Gaussian broadening saturates R at ≈+1 with no R1≠R2 — never the observed +2. R is largest for the SHARPEST PSFs (most singular deconvolution) and tracks the core profile residual. A clean point source through the same machinery gives R≈0, so the estimator is not broken for a perfect PSF — but no fittable PSF model avoids it: a real PSFEx model fit on the stars, at three fidelities (default, higher degree, bright-trained), leaves ~2/3 of bright stars catastrophic, no better than the truth PSF, while only the exact star (C_self) reaches ~0. The limitation is the interaction of the near-point-source regime with any imperfect, modeled PSF, near-singular under metacal's deconvolution.

self-contained PSF-stamp experiments: minutes each on one node
size-offset2nd-moment size offset (the star being ~0.7% broader)
A real but insufficient contributor — a symptom of the profile mismatch, not the whole cause.		demoted

Demoted (not dismissed). On a fixed PSF, a controlled pure-size broadening drives the response from 0 up to ≈+1 — a real, large effect — but saturates there and produces no unequal-component asymmetry, while the real star on the same PSF reaches +2.2 with a strong asymmetry. So size supplies about half the climb; the profile mismatch supplies the rest. Across fields the size offset no longer predicts the response once they sit at the multi-epoch ceiling. Size is a symptom of the underlying profile mismatch, not the driver.

fit-breakdownBright-star fit breakdown (noise/weight model)
Reduced chi-square rises to ~8 at the bright end; the model mis-fits high-S/N stars.		leading

Reduced chi-square climbs from ~0.22 (faint) to ~8 (mag 14–15), co-located with the R climb, and correlates with |R1| (ρ=+0.13). The faint-end value <1 means the noise is over-estimated there (matching Fabian's chi-square ~0.1) while bright stars are under-fit. Amplifies the divergence but does not fully explain it (even best-fit bright stars diverge), so this is a contributing mechanism, not the whole story. Deciding test: add the real noise/weight model to the controlled point-source experiment.

psf-handoffWrong PSF passed to the shape fitter
The PSF the pipeline removes differs from the one that made the images.		ruled out

Ruled out. The deconvolution PSF stamps are byte-identical to the render PSF across all checked fields (max difference 0). The directional asymmetry must arise after the hand-off, inside the metacalibration.

coordinate-offsetCoordinate / inter-exposure offset
Mis-propagated image coordinates distort the response.		ruled out

Ruled out as the driver. A deliberately wrong offset (known A/B pair) leaves R and size unchanged to ~1%; the measured star size stays ~0 (an offset bug would inflate it); and the climb persists with a single epoch, where there is no inter-exposure offset to propagate.

reconv-kernelMetacalibration reconvolution kernel choice
The internal kernel used to re-blur after shearing.		ruled out

Ruled out as the climb's driver, but it governs robustness. The default fit-a-Gaussian kernel (what the pipeline uses) is ~3–5× noisier in R and carries a few-% catastrophic |R|>1 tail even when the model matches the star exactly; a fixed round Gaussian kernel removes both. Neither changes the bright-end climb (the input-PSF response stays ≈+2 under both), so the kernel calibrates the zero and the catastrophic fraction, not the climb.

#DiagnosticStatusNote

Yes. A deliberately-wrong inter-exposure offset (a known A/B pair) leaves the response and size unchanged to ~1%, so coordinate propagation does not drive the climb. (The A/B fields are galaxies, not bright stars; the star case is covered by the size staying ~0, which an offset bug would inflate.)

2Watch a star acquire a response in the metacal stampsto do

Dump the reconvolved post-metacalibration stamps and the difference across shear branches for a few bright stars, to see directly how a near-point source picks up a directional response. Needs a twin run that saves the intermediate stamps.

3Does the PSF used match the PSF that made the images?done

Yes, exactly. The PSF stamps the pipeline deconvolves by are byte-identical to the render PSF across all checked fields (max difference 0). The hand-off carries no error.

4Do the two PSF measurements agree?done

The pipeline now fits the original image PSF independently of the metacalibration reconvolution kernel (the older code copied one into the other). On the rerun they agree in shape (both round) and differ ~10% in size — the expected metacalibration dilation, not an inconsistency.

Open questions

  • Is the bright-star climb a benign property of the near-point-source regime rather than a shear-calibration problem? Stars are near-point sources — the pathological regime for the deconvolution — while the resolved galaxies that carry the cosmic-shear signal sit away from the singularity. Test: measure the response for the resolved galaxies in the same sims (does it stay near zero?), and check whether down-weighting or excluding the brightest stars cleans the diagnostic without touching the galaxy calibration.

  • Can a PSF model OUTSIDE the PSFEx pixel basis narrow the catastrophic tail? A real PSFEx model at three fidelities (default, higher degree, bright-trained) leaves ~2/3 of bright stars catastrophic — no better than the truth PSF — because a pixel basis cannot represent a near-point-source profile faithfully enough and adds high-frequency deconvolution instability. An analytic Gauss-Laguerre (shapelet) basis is the most likely model class to reduce the blow-ups. A clean oversampling test also remains open: mapping an oversampled PSFEx model to the detector grid carries a ~0.8% size ambiguity, so the oversampled run was inconclusive; calibrating that resample to the truth-PSF size would settle whether oversampling helps at all.

  • Does switching the pipeline's re-blurring kernel from the default fit-a-Gaussian to a fixed round Gaussian reduce the catastrophic fraction on the real star catalogues? On the twin it removes the few-% exact-match tail and tightens the response ~3–5× without touching the climb; a single-module rerun with that one setting changed is the cheap confirmation on real data.

  • Why does the response divide unequally between the two shear components (R1 larger than R2) for a round star? The directional part of the profile mismatch is the natural candidate (the fitted processing kernel is directionally asymmetric, and removing it removes the asymmetry); a pure round broadening does not produce it.

  • Why is the noise over-estimated for faint stars (reduced chi-square ~0.15) yet the bright stars under-fit (reduced chi-square ~8)? Is a single noise/weight mis-normalization behind both? (Amplifier, not driver.)

  • In the metacalibration stamps, how does a near-point source pick up a directional response — show the reconvolved stamps and the difference across shear branches for a few bright stars (Fabian's ask).
